tagline: From Cumberland Gap to country music along Kentucky’s historic travel corridor.
intro: The Wilderness Road Heritage Highway links Cumberland Gap country with Renfro Valley and Berea over 93.8 miles. At its southern end, Middlesboro lies between Pine Mountain and the Cumberland Mountains; farther north, Pineville occupies a narrow strip between mountain and river. FHWA lists this National Scenic Byway as a two-hour drive, highlighting its settlement and Civil War history, country music and Berea’s crafts.

In 1775, the Transylvania Company hired Daniel Boone to widen the path through Cumberland Gap for settlers bound for Kentucky and Tennessee. The early Wilderness Road admitted walkers and riders; Kentucky’s legislature funded improvements in 1792, and an all-weather wagon road opened in 1796. Modern highways follow much of that route, with realignments separating them from the old trails. A paved macadam road through the gap was completed in 1908 and later became US 25E. A tunnel took traffic beneath the gap in 1996; restoration of the original trail followed.

Traveling north from Middlesboro, US 25E reaches Pineville and then Barbourville in the Cumberland River valley. At London, US 25 serves as Main Street and continues toward Mount Vernon. Renfro Valley lies north of Mount Vernon; beyond it, US 25 carries the journey into the center of Berea.

moments.title: Cumberland Gap
moments.text: Cumberland Gap cuts a V through the mountain ridge near the meeting of Kentucky, Virginia and Tennessee. Native American nations used the passage long before Boone’s party widened the path in 1775. Its later life as a highway changed again in 1996, when the Cumberland Gap Tunnel replaced the overland US 25E crossing. The original trail was then restored within Cumberland Gap National Historical Park. The gap sits at 1,631 feet above sea level, with Pinnacle Overlook rising on its north side. The park also has many hiking trails through this mountain landscape.
moments.notice: Notice the V-shaped break in the Cumberland Mountain ridgeline.

moments.title: Pineville
moments.text: Pineville began at a river crossing: the Wilderness Road met the Cumberland here, and the settlement took the name Cumberland Ford in 1781. Renamed Pineville in 1870, the town occupies a small strip of land between the river and Pine Mountain. That riverside position has also exposed it to floods. In April 1977, water overwhelmed the floodwall built in 1952, damaging or destroying 200 houses. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers upgraded the wall in 1988. US 25E passes through town directly north of the river’s water gap through Pine Mountain.

moments.title: Renfro Valley
moments.text: At Renfro Valley, country music traveled from a local stage onto the CBS Radio Network. John Lair and others founded the entertainment center in 1939; its Barn Dance gave Hank Williams, Red Foley and other performers an early spotlight. CBS carried programming from the valley until the late 1950s. The Gatherin’ began its Sunday broadcasts in September 1943 and moved into recorded syndication after CBS stopped carrying it. Renfro Valley’s own entertainers continue to put on stage shows. The neighborhood, north of Mount Vernon on US 25, is also home to the Kentucky Music Hall of Fame and Museum.
